passages.happening:
The speeches are finished. “Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which faces Jericho” (verse 1).

There God showed him the whole land. The list sweeps round it: Gilead as far as Dan in the north, Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, all Judah as far as the Western Sea, the Negev in the south, and the valley of Jericho as far as Zoar (verses 1-3).

God said to him, ‘This is the land that I swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’. Then: ‘I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
After thirty-three chapters of Moses' voice, the narrator speaks again, quietly. The poetry is over. The telling is plain.

Mount Nebo is traditionally placed on a ridge in what is now the country of Jordan. On a clear day it gives a view across the Jordan valley toward Jericho and the hills of Judah. Pisgah seems to be the name of the peak or of the ridge it belongs to.

The places named run in a rough circle round the whole land, from the far north to the far south and to the Mediterranean Sea. No one could see all of that with the naked eye from any mountain. Many readers take the sight as something God gave and not as what a man's eyes could reach.

God's words tie this moment to the beginning of the story. The land is the one sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Moses is shown that the promise made centuries before is about to be kept. He is the last person in the five books to hear it.

And then the sentence he has known was coming: ‘you will not cross into it’. He asked once and was told not to ask again. Now he stands and looks.

There is kindness in the scene. God does not send him away to die out of sight of the land. He takes him up and shows him all of it, piece by piece, naming the places as a guide would. Moses does not enter. But he sees that it is real, and that it is there.
passages.later:
The promise Moses hears goes back to God's first appearance to Abraham in the land: “I will give this land to your offspring” (Genesis 12:7).

The letter to the Hebrews describes people of faith in words that fit Moses on the mountain: “All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13).
passages.asks: Moses saw what he had worked for and did not enter it. Ask what you are working toward that others, and not you, may enjoy. And ask whether you can thank God for being shown the promise, even where you are not the one to receive it.

passages.t: The death and burial of Moses
passages.happening:
“So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, as the LORD had said” (verse 5).

“And He buried him in a valley in the land of Moab facing Beth-peor, and no one to this day knows the location of his grave” (verse 6).

“Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not weak, and his vitality had not diminished” (verse 7).

“The Israelites grieved for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the time of weeping and mourning for Moses came to an end” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The death is told in one sentence, without any speech. Moses says nothing. After a whole book of his words, he is silent.

He is given a title: ‘the servant of the LORD’. It is the highest the Old Testament gives him. To be the servant of a great king was an honor. It meant belonging to the king and acting for him. The man who is kept out of the land dies with that name.

‘He buried him.’ The one who buries Moses is God. No family carried him to a tomb. Burial mattered greatly in the ancient world, and a person was laid with his ancestors where he could. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lie together in one cave. Moses has no such place. He dies outside the land, alone on a mountain, and God himself lays him in the ground.

No one knows where. One result is that no shrine could grow up around his grave, and no one could make the tomb of Moses a place to worship.

He did not die of weakness. His eyes were clear and his strength was whole. He died, verse 5 says, ‘as the LORD had said’.

Israel wept for thirty days, as it had wept for Aaron. Then the weeping ‘came to an end’. The book does not hurry the grief, and it does not let grief have the last word. There is a river to cross.

This is a sad page, and it should be allowed to be sad. The greatest leader in Israel's story dies with his work unfinished, within sight of the place he longed for. The Bible does not tidy that away. It lets the people weep. It also shows how he died: known by God, called his servant, shown the promise, and buried by God's own hand.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua opens with God's own notice of the death, and with the next step: “Moses My servant is dead. Now therefore arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan” (Joshua 1:2).

The letter to the Hebrews honors Moses with the title of verse 5: “Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house, testifying to what would be spoken later” (Hebrews 3:5).

And the Gospels show him once more. On a mountain inside the land, ‘two men, Moses and Elijah, began talking with Jesus’ (Luke 9:30). They ‘spoke about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem’ (Luke 9:31).
passages.hard:
Is it right to grieve over a death like this, and what does it say to someone who is grieving?

Israel grieved for thirty days, and the text records it without any rebuke. Grief is the fitting answer to a death, even the death of an old man who had lived a full life and died as God's servant. Nothing in the Bible asks a believer to pretend otherwise.

The chapter also does not say that a life is wasted if its hopes are not all fulfilled. Moses did not get what he longed for, and he is honored above every prophet who came after him.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God buried Moses himself, where no one would ever find the grave. Ask what it means to you that God attends to the death of his servants. And if you are grieving someone, let the thirty days stand. Ask whether you have given your grief the time it needs.

passages.t: ‘No prophet has risen in Israel like Moses’
passages.happening:
“Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses” (verse 9).

Then the book looks back. “Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (verse 10). No prophet did such signs and wonders as God sent Moses to do in Egypt (verse 11), and none ‘performed all the mighty acts of power and awesome deeds that Moses did in the sight of all Israel’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The work goes on. Joshua has been made ready. The laying on of hands was the sign by which authority was passed to a successor. God gives Joshua ‘the spirit of wisdom’, which in the Old Testament means the practical skill to live and lead under God. The people follow him. The promise did not depend on Moses, and it crosses the river without him.

Then the last three verses, which are the last words of the five books of Moses.

They say that Moses was unlike any prophet after him. The mark of the difference is given: the LORD knew him ‘face to face’. Other prophets received visions and dreams. With Moses God spoke directly and plainly. Exodus says it was ‘as a man speaks to his friend’. The phrase does not mean that Moses saw all of God's glory, which Exodus says no one can see and live. It means that nothing stood between them when God spoke.

The words ‘since that time’ show that these verses were written looking back, after other prophets had come and gone. The writer has seen them and says that none was the equal of Moses.

So the Torah ends with an open door. In chapter 18 God promised to raise up a prophet like Moses. The last page says that he has not yet come. The five books close with the reader still waiting.

With this chapter the five books of Moses are complete: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. They began with God making the heavens and the earth. They end with a people at a river, a promise still ahead of them, and a grave that only God can find.
passages.later:
Exodus describes the closeness that verse 10 remembers: “Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11).

Numbers tells how Joshua was made ready: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the Spirit in him, and lay your hands on him” (Numbers 27:18).

In the time of Jesus people were still asking whether the prophet had come: “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6:14). Peter told a crowd in Jerusalem that Jesus is the one Moses spoke of (Acts 3:22). The note on chapter 18, verses 15 to 22, sets out how Jewish and Christian readers understand the promise.

The letter to the Hebrews sets Moses and Jesus side by side, with honor to both: “Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house”. “But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house” (Hebrews 3:5-6).
passages.hard:
Who wrote the account of the death of Moses?

The question is very old. Moses could not have written of his own death and burial, or of the thirty days of mourning that followed, or the judgment that no prophet like him had arisen ‘since that time’.

A Jewish tradition recorded in the Talmud gives the last eight verses of Deuteronomy to Joshua. Others have suggested a later editor. The words ‘to this day’ in verse 6 suggest that at least those lines were written some time after the events.

Most readers accept that someone other than Moses recorded his death. That includes many who hold that Moses is the author of the five books as a whole. It is one of the plainest signs in the Bible that the books of Moses reached their present form through more hands than one.

How much more of the five books comes from later hands is a larger question, on which Christians who confess the Bible as God's word hold different views. The book introduction sets them out, and so does the site's page on who wrote the first five books. These notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: The five books end with the people still waiting for a prophet like Moses. Ask what you are waiting for from God, and whether you can wait as Israel was asked to: with the promise in hand and the river still ahead. And look back over the whole of this book. Ask what one thing Moses said that you most need to remember.
